notes: Comparative synthesis arguing that basic principles of locomotor network organization are conserved between vertebrates and invertebrates, permitting mechanistic study at multiple physiological levels; sensory signals and neuromodulatory input reconfigure network properties, and these networks reorganize in response to nervous-system injury.
animal_study: Test the conserved-principles claim directly: apply the same phase-specific afferent stimulation or neuromodulatory perturbation to locomotor networks in one vertebrate and one invertebrate preparation and compare the network-level reconfiguration.
robot_sim: Implement CPG networks whose properties are reconfigurable by simulated neuromodulatory and sensory inputs, then reproduce the reported reorganization after simulated injury (partial deafferentation or transection) as a benchmark for recovery mechanisms.

notes: Reviews the C. elegans ventral nerve cord motor circuit — its architecture, development, fate-specifying genes, and models of locomotor control — and identifies surprising structural and developmental similarities between the nematode and vertebrate axial nerve cords, speculating that conserved transcription factor families shaped the evolution of both motor circuits.
animal_study: Test the speculated conservation: knock down or knock out the conserved transcription factor families in a vertebrate preparation and assay whether motor neuron fate specification and circuit organization parallel the nematode sequence.
flags: Animal preparation is C. elegans (nematode) — no matching name in the allowed animals vocabulary; animals left empty.

notes: A 3-D digital reconstruction of 27 cat hindlimb motoneuron pools, modulated by compiled EMG profiles, reveals a rostrocaudal oscillation of spinal activity across the step cycle: the caudal third of the lumbosacral enlargement dominates during stance, activation shifts abruptly rostral during swing, and a transient caudal focus at the stance-swing transition coincides with retractor muscles (gracilis, posterior biceps, semimembranosus, semitendinosus) that clear the foot from the ground.
animal_study: Run the designed follow-up: characterize the same spatiotemporal MN activation in a spinalized, deafferented preparation (no descending or sensory inputs) and compare with the intact pattern to isolate the CPG-internal spatiotemporal structure.
robot_sim: Distribute a simulated cat-scale MN pool model rostrocaudally per these digitized coordinates and phase-modulate the pools with EMG-derived profiles; test whether the rostrocaudal oscillation and the caudal stance-swing transition focus emerge, and how they degrade when sensory inputs are ablated.

notes: The CASE/NPS Beach Whegs robot demonstrates abstracted biological inspiration in practice: terrain-adaptive gaits emerge passively from insect-inspired mechanics, so the robot carries no gait sensors and its controller only issues speed and heading directives — evidence that morphological computation can replace explicit terrain-feedback control.
animal_study: Test the passive-adaptation claim on rapid-running insects: run them across graded heterogeneous terrain after disruption of leg afferent input and quantify how much terrain adaptation survives, separating preflexive mechanics from active sensory control.
robot_sim: Replicate the design principle in simulation: a legged model whose passive mechanics adapt gait to terrain with all gait sensors ablated, mapping which terrain classes are handled purely preflexively and where active control becomes necessary.

notes: Microstimulation of the cat medullary reticular formation during locomotion evokes phase-dependent responses incorporated into the ongoing pattern — flexor excitation in each limb during that muscle's natural activity period, inhibition of ipsilateral extensors, mixed responses in contralateral vastus lateralis — with response latencies shortest during a muscle's active period, showing that reticulospinal transmission is gated by the locomotor network itself.
animal_study: Repeat the stimulation protocol in deafferented or fictively locomoting preparations to determine how much of the phase-dependent gating of reticulospinal effects is produced centrally by the locomotor network versus by phasic sensory feedback.
robot_sim: Implement descending reticulospinal-like drive onto a CPG with phase-dependent pathway gating (gain high during each muscle's active phase) and reproduce the shortening of response latency with activity state as a test of state-dependent transmission.

notes: During MLR-evoked fictive locomotion in the decerebrate cat, midlumbar (L4) interneurons receiving group II input from quadriceps, sartorius, and pretibial flexors — and projecting to L7 motor nuclei — fired predominantly with ipsilateral flexor bursts and were less responsive to peripheral input during extension: a phase-gated group II pathway positioned to shape flexor activity.
animal_study: Test the pathway's causal role by reversibly silencing the identified L4 interneurons, or their group II input, during fictive locomotion and measuring changes in flexor burst timing and in the phase gating of peripheral responsiveness.
robot_sim: Implement a midlumbar interneuron layer receiving group II afferent input from quadriceps, sartorius, and pretibial flexor pathways and projecting to motor nuclei, with gain reduced during extension; test its contribution to flexor burst generation in a CPG model.
flags: Group II afferent-to-midlumbar-interneuron-to-motor-nucleus pathway demonstrated, but the sign of the action on motoneurons is not stated in the abstract — no exact feedback vocabulary fit; feedback left empty.

notes: Extends energy-balance and perturbation analysis from smooth dynamical systems to the phase-discontinuous (hybrid) dynamics of legged hopping, predicting existence and stability of vertical-hopper limit cycles; predictions match simulated true values for both linear and nonlinear models, providing a low-cost stability certificate for hybrid locomotion systems.
robot_sim: Use the energy-balance perturbation method to certify limit-cycle existence and stability of hopper and CPG-driven walker models (linear and nonlinear variants) before closed-loop or hardware testing, as validated here against simulation.

notes: In decerebrate and spinal cats, fictive locomotor cycle period varied predominantly with the extension phase while the flexion phase stayed relatively invariant; this walking-speed asymmetry (stance varies, swing constant) persisted without phasic sensory feedback, supraspinal structures, pharmacology, or sustained stimulation, establishing it as an intrinsic property of spinal CPG organization.
animal_study: Quantify how extraneous factors reshape the intrinsic asymmetry: apply phasic afferent stimulation, monoaminergic drugs, or sustained drive during fictive locomotion and measure whether dominance of extension-duration control shifts.
robot_sim: Build a half-center CPG whose cycle period is modulated primarily through extension (stance) duration with swing duration near-invariant; verify the asymmetry survives removal of all simulated sensory feedback, then add feedback to test modulation.

notes: Review of mammalian spinal central pattern generators emphasizing that one spinal cord produces multiple rhythmic behaviors — walking, running, swimming, scratching — each with its own goals and demands, and discussing how spinal circuitry is organized to deliver this complexity and flexibility.
animal_study: Test shared-versus-dedicated circuitry: record the same spinal interneurons during walking and scratching in the same animal to determine which elements are common across rhythmic behaviors and which are behavior-specific.
robot_sim: Implement a modular CPG architecture that recombines shared rhythm- and pattern-formation elements to generate multiple distinct rhythmic output sets, testing whether one network reproduces the different behaviors' demands.

notes: Argues through four case studies that adaptive behavior is best obtained by exploiting embodied dynamics rather than suppressing them: evolved analog electronic controllers act as robot controllers, insect-inspired navigation builds on innate behaviors, neuromechanical chaos powers a goal-driven search for robust motor behaviors with neural-oscillator architectures, and evolved dynamical controllers yield agile flapping flight robust to wind gusts.
animal_study: For the navigation case: manipulate the visual information supplied by innate behaviors in insect experiments to test the claim that rapid route learning depends on navigation-specific visual information exploited by those innate behaviors.
robot_sim: Adopt the neuromechanical-chaos result: use neural-oscillator controllers whose chaotic dynamics power a goal-driven search for motor behaviors, testing whether robust locomotion emerges by exploiting rather than damping body-level chaos.

notes: Shows theoretically and in simulation that control laws can be geometrically encoded in the feedforward trajectories of appendages, giving deadbeat stability in hybrid legged models: a simplified vertical hopper rejects ground-height changes without sensing the ground. Cautions that control identified in an existing animal or machine may reside in such geometric stabilization rather than neural or computational feedback.
animal_study: Test the caution in running animals: block distal sensory feedback while systematically varying terrain height and test whether feedforward appendage trajectory shaping alone preserves stability — a positive result would indicate geometric, non-neural stabilization.
robot_sim: Encode a desired control law into the open-loop joint trajectories of a simulated hopper or legged model, remove all feedback loops, and verify deadbeat stability and ground-height rejection as achieved here with little or no sensing.
flags: Geometric/feedforward stabilization without sensing — conceptually adjacent to 'Biomechanically mediated preflexive feedback' but explicitly not feedback; feedback vocabulary left empty.

notes: Proposes a 'mechanics space' in which limb size and limb speed determine the dominant mechanical regime: inertia-dominated (large, fast limbs — muscle work becomes kinetic energy, requiring compensatory control and active damping), gravity/elastic-dominated (small, slow — compensatory control and active damping unnecessary), and viscous-dominated (small, fast — joint viscosity alone yields exclusively stable motion). Neural control strategy is thus set almost entirely by limb scale and speed.
animal_study: Test the framework's predictions across scale: perturb or partially disrupt active neural control in animals whose limbs fall in different mechanics-space regions and test whether stability losses occur only in the inertia-dominated regime.
robot_sim: Scale a limb model through the mechanics space and vary active damping and compensatory control accordingly; verify that stability persists without active control in the elastic and viscous regimes but is lost in the inertia regime without it.

notes: Critical review arguing that rhythmic leg-muscle activity elicited in severe spinal cord injury by assisted treadmill stepping reflects entrainment of spinal proprioceptive reflex circuits by cyclically generated proprioceptive feedback rather than central pattern generator activation, and that genuine CPG engagement requires sustained tonic excitatory drive — from electrical spinal cord stimulation or combinations of dopaminergic, adrenergic, and 5-HT pharmacology.
animal_study: Dissociate the two mechanisms in a spinalized animal model: deliver tonic drive (epidural stimulation or monoamine agonists) and phasic limb movement independently and in combination, testing whether rhythmic output requires tonic drive while phasic feedback alone merely entrains reflex circuits.
robot_sim: Implement a lumbar circuit model with separately controlled reflex entrainment (cyclic proprioceptive input drives reflex circuits) and CPG activation (tonic excitatory drive gates rhythm generation); reproduce the dissociation and test rehabilitation-style combined stimulation.
flags: No feedback vocabulary entry for 'entrainment of spinal reflex circuits by cyclic proprioceptive feedback' — candidate new term for Ben.

notes: Disrupting plantarflexor proprioception with noisy Achilles tendon vibration left level walking largely unchanged but slowed adaptation to a 2.5% incline — shorter stride periods and redistributed medial gastrocnemius activity (reduced mid-stance, increased late-stance) persisted for 2-3 minutes before converging, and uphill metabolic cost rose — indicating proprioceptive feedback is needed to rapidly identify low-cost muscle activation patterns.
animal_study: Replicate in an animal model: apply tendon vibration or selectively silence ankle extensor proprioception during locomotion on changing inclines and measure adaptation rate, redistribution of muscle activation, and metabolic cost.
robot_sim: Add a proprioception-dependent adaptation layer to a neuromuscular gait model that searches for economical activation patterns; ablate the proprioceptive input and reproduce the delayed adaptation and elevated cost under a mechanical demand change.
flags: Afferent type behind the vibration-disrupted 'proprioception' is not specified in the abstract (tendon vibration typically implicates Ia) — afferents left empty.

notes: A multi-muscle biomechanical model analyzed across size scales shows that constituent hip torques (inertial, passive viscoelastic) shift in relative importance with animal size, predicting that extensor and flexor activation phases invert between small and large sizes executing the same kinematic motion — a scale-dependent principle for neural control strategy consistent with documented hindlimb torque during locomotion.
animal_study: Validate the predicted activation-phase inversion by recording hip extensor and flexor EMG in animals spanning large size scales performing matched kinematics, comparing observed phase relationships with the model's constituent-torque predictions.
robot_sim: Embed the scale-dependent torque analysis in a simulated multi-muscle limb: sweep size-scale, recompute the required extensor/flexor activation phasing, and verify the predicted phase flip and agreement with documented hindlimb torque profiles.

notes: In the cockroach, which can generate coordinated leg patterns without sensory feedback, imposed transient and periodic movements of a single intact leg phase-dependently modified phase relationships among other legs' segmental oscillators: front-leg feedback is weaker but more phase-precise than hind-leg feedback, selectively strengthening the inherent rhythmic pattern while modulating local perturbations — proprioception reinforces rather than replaces the central pattern.
animal_study: Identify and selectively ablate the leg proprioceptors mediating the effect, then impose single-leg transient and periodic movements to quantify how front- versus hind-leg feedback strength and phase precision shape inter-leg coordination.
robot_sim: Implement hexapod segmental oscillators with leg-local proprioceptive feedback that adjusts inter-oscillator coupling, giving front legs lower gain but tighter phase precision; ablate the feedback to test degradation of pattern robustness to local perturbations.
flags: Inter-leg proprioceptive reinforcement of the central pattern in cockroach — sensory organs and afferent types not named in the abstract; no exact feedback vocabulary fit.

notes: During human air-stepping, which removes foot-contact interactions, four NMF-extracted motor modules activated sequentially, with reconstructed motoneuron clusters progressing from rostral to caudal spinal regions from initial flexion to the last extension phase — evidence for rostrocaudally traveling waves in human locomotor spinal circuits, resolving the rostral propagation shift previously observed at foot contact during walking.
animal_study: Record spinal or muscle activity in an animal model during air-stepping versus grounded stepping to separate the CPG-internal rostrocaudal wave sequence from sensory effects of foot contact.
robot_sim: Implement a rostrocaudally sequenced motor-module CPG (a traveling wave over distributed MN pools) and reproduce the module activation order from initial flexion to late extension during unloaded stepping, then add ground contact to test waveform modulation.

notes: The spring-loaded inverted pendulum alone cannot explain the dynamic stability of walking and running in many physically relevant parameter ranges; adding realistic hip-motor clock torques yields the clock-torqued CT-SLIP, which captures the robust stability observed in most animals and legged robots — feedforward clock-like actuation, not passive spring dynamics alone, underwrites gait stability.
animal_study: Test the model's implication in animals: measure stability boundaries under systematic parameter variation (speed, effective stiffness) and test whether CT-SLIP rather than passive SLIP predicts the observed robustness.
robot_sim: Implement CT-SLIP (a lossy SLIP with clock-torqued hip actuation) and map its stability properties against passive SLIP across parameter ranges, using it as the whole-body center-of-mass layer for legged locomotion controllers.

notes: Adding gait-patterned lower-limb muscle vibration to a first-person walking avatar increased static participants' sense of agency and illusory perception of walking; only realistic, temporally aligned proprioceptive stimulation produced anteroposterior center-of-pressure sway matching the avatar's gait cadence — congruent proprioceptive input alone can evoke motor correlates of gait.

Brief electrical stimulation of cutaneous nerves during cat treadmill locomotion evoked phase-gated short-latency reflexes — inhibition of extensors and excitation of flexors, expressed only during locomotor phases in which the respective motoneuron pools were active — while longer-latency components were gated similarly but not identically, indicating partial independence from the basic locomotor drive on the pool.
animal_study: Extend to fictive locomotion to test whether the phase-dependent gating of these cutaneous reflexes persists without movement-related afferent feedback, isolating central pattern control of reflex gain; and map additional distal nerves with the graphical gating technique.
robot_sim: Implement phase-gated cutaneous reflex pathways — flexor excitation and extensor inhibition enabled only during each pool's active locomotor phase, with separately gated late components — and test perturbation responses across the step cycle.

notes: Introduces a dendritic neuron model with nonlinear synapses trained by six metaheuristic algorithms (biogeography-based optimization, particle swarm, genetic algorithm, ant colony, evolutionary strategy, population-based incremental learning), outperforming a multilayer perceptron across 14 classification, approximation, and prediction tasks — a biologically motivated unit for practical machine learning rather than a systems-level motor model.
flags: Off-topic for a sensory afferent database: pure machine-learning neuron-model paper with no afferent or locomotor content — Ben may want to reclassify or drop.

notes: Combining a computational model of cat locomotion with experiments shows that after thoracic lateral hemisection the contralesional ('intact') side remains governed mainly by supraspinal drives while the ipsilesional side is dominated by somatosensory feedback; simulations correctly predicted changes in cycle and phase durations during tied-belt and split-belt locomotion, and placing the ipsilesional hindlimb on the slow belt substantially reduced the effects of hemisection.
animal_study: Causally test the model's division of control by selectively deafferenting the ipsilesional hindlimb after hemisection (predicted loss of ipsilesional stepping), and by swapping belt-speed assignment to manipulate the slow-belt protective effect.
robot_sim: Simulate hemisection in a two-level CPG model by removing descending drive to one side; test whether ipsilesional stepping is sustained by somatosensory feedback alone, and reproduce the reduction of hemisection effects when the ipsilesional limb steps on the slow belt during split-belt locomotion.

notes: Proposes central pattern generator models built from coupled neural oscillators trained by simultaneous-perturbation learning that uses only CPG outputs — avoiding backpropagation-style internal-error propagation — including a complex-valued CPG that learned and controlled ten joint angles of a humanoid robot for walking and stepping motion patterns.
robot_sim: Apply output-only simultaneous-perturbation tuning to a neural-oscillator CPG controlling a simulated biped's joints, reproducing learned walking and stepping waveforms as an alternative to gradient-based parameter fitting.

notes: Develops multiplierless digital variants of the biological adaptive-exponential neuron model that reproduce different biological firing behaviors with high precision at considerably lower FPGA implementation cost than the original model, enabling large-scale, low-cost digital simulation of biologically realistic spiking networks.
robot_sim: Deploy the low-cost adaptive-exponential neuron variants as hardware neuron units in a real-time neural controller and verify their firing behaviors against the original model to confirm performance parity at reduced implementation cost.
flags: Off-topic for a sensory afferent database: digital hardware neuron implementation with no afferent or locomotor content — Ben may want to reclassify.

notes: In clonidine-treated acute and chronic spinal cats, group I stimulation of the plantaris nerve entrained the locomotor rhythm and, during locomotor activity, group Ib afferents from plantaris exerted an excitatory action on medial gastrocnemius bursts (30-50 ms latency) through the extensor half-center of the rhythm generator — reversing the inhibitory effect the same stimuli produced on tonic activity without locomotion; selective Ia activation by muscle vibration neither entrained the rhythm nor augmented the bursts.
animal_study: Identify and reversibly inactivate the interneurons mediating the locomotor Ib reversal, then test extensor burst timing and rhythm entrainment under controlled plantaris loading across locomotor and non-locomotor states.
robot_sim: Implement state-dependent Ib feedback in a half-center CPG: autogenic inhibition at rest switching to excitation of the extensor half-center during locomotion, with rhythm entrainment by group I stimulation but not by Ia-specific input; ablate the reversal to test loss of load-dependent stance burst augmentation.
